title: The chords in your key
summary: Roman numerals, four minor-key progressions that turn up in beat after beat and the moods they carry, and the borrowed V chord that adds tension.

steps.title: Numbers, not names
steps.body:
Musicians often name chords by number, not letter. Each chord gets the **Roman numeral** of the scale note it's built on: I for the 1st, IV for the 4th, and so on. Lowercase means minor, uppercase major, ° diminished.

In any minor key that gives: **i, ii°, III, iv, v, VI, VII**.

Why numbers? They work in every key. **i–VI** is Am to F in A minor, and Cm to Ab in C minor: the same sound, moved. Your pads show both name and numeral, so any progression here works in your key.

Next: four progressions you'll hear all over minor-key beats.
steps.deeper:
The full set in A minor:

- **i** Am (A C E)
- **ii°** Bdim (B D F)
- **III** C (C E G)
- **iv** Dm (D F A)
- **v** Em (E G B)
- **VI** F (F A C)
- **VII** G (G B D)

A progression written in numerals is a recipe; the key picks the ingredients. i–iv–v is Am–Dm–Em in A minor, Em–Am–Bm in E minor, and Fm–Bbm–Cm in F minor.

These numerals come from the **natural minor** scale, the one your key uses. The last part of this lesson adds one chord from outside it.

steps.title: Four progressions to know
steps.body:
A few progressions turn up again and again in minor-key beats:

- **i–VI**: two chords, back and forth. Dark and hypnotic, with lots of room for a vocal.
- **i–VI–III–VII**: three major chords after the home chord. More emotional, a little hopeful.
- **i–iv–v**: all minor. Dark from start to finish.
- **i–iv–VI–v**: dark, with one brighter chord (VI) before the v pulls it back down.

All four start on **i**, so every pass of the loop begins at home.

Next: i–VI against i–VI–III–VII.
steps.deeper:
In A minor:

- i–VI: **Am–F**
- i–VI–III–VII: **Am–F–C–G**
- i–iv–v: **Am–Dm–Em**
- i–iv–VI–v: **Am–Dm–F–Em**

Why i–VI sounds so smooth: Am (A C E) and F (F A C) share two notes, A and C. Only one note really changes, E to F, so the move is soft and the mood stays put.

Am–F–C–G uses the same four chords as the well-known pop progression C–G–Am–F, just started from Am. Starting on Am makes it the home chord, so the same chords sound darker.

Moods come from the chord qualities: the more minor chords, the darker it stays; each major chord adds light. Tempo, sound and melody shift the mood too, so treat these as starting points.

steps.title: Two chords vs four
steps.caption: Same drums, one chord per bar. Bars 1 and 2 are the same in both: Am, then F. Listen to bars 3 and 4.

examples.label: i–VI
examples.explanation: Am, F, Am, F. Home and VI rocking back and forth. It stays dark and leaves the space open.

examples.label: i–VI–III–VII
examples.explanation: Am, F, then C and G. Two more major chords lift it, and G steps up into Am when the loop comes back round.

steps.title: All minor vs one bright chord
steps.caption: Same drums, same first two bars: Am, then Dm. Only bar 3 differs.

examples.label: i–iv–v
examples.explanation: Am, Dm, then Em for two bars. Every chord is minor, so nothing brightens it.

examples.label: i–iv–VI–v
examples.explanation: Am, Dm, F, Em. The F in bar 3 is major: a moment of light before Em takes it back down.

steps.title: The borrowed V
steps.body:
In your key, the chord on the 5th note is minor: **v**. In A minor that's Em (E, G, B). Raise its middle note a half step, G to **G#**, and you get **V**: E major (E, G#, B).

G# sits a half step below A, the home note, so it pulls hard toward it. Put V at the end of the loop and the restart on **i** lands like a release.

The G# comes from **harmonic minor**, which you met in Stage 1, so the pad says **V ·borrowed**. Add a 7th, **E7**, for even more pull.

Next: the same loop ending on v, V, then V7.
steps.deeper:
A minor is A B C D E F G. **Harmonic minor** raises the 7th note: A B C D E F G#. Build the chord on the 5th with that G# and you get **E** (E G# B), or **E7** (E G# B D) with a 7th on top.

A note a half step below home is called the **leading tone**, because it leads into home. In natural minor, G is a whole step below A, so v drifts back to i softly. G# is only a half step away, so V pulls back strongly.

In E7 a second note resolves too: D steps down to C, the middle note of Am.

V to i is the classic way minor-key music says "back home". Keeping v minor sounds darker and less pushy; V sounds more dramatic.

G# isn't in your key's scale, so in a melody it can sound wrong unless V is under it. This lesson's key check accepts V and V7 in minor keys.

steps.title: v, V and V7
steps.caption: Same drums, same first three bars: Am, Dm, F. Only the last chord changes. Listen to the moment the loop jumps back to Am.

examples.label: Ends on v: Em
examples.explanation: E, G, B, straight from your key. It slides back to Am gently.

examples.label: Ends on V: E
examples.explanation: One note changes: G becomes G#. That G# rises a half step to A as Am comes back, and the restart feels like an arrival.

examples.label: Ends on V7: E7
examples.explanation: E, G#, B, plus D. Now two notes lean home: G# up to A, and D down to C. The strongest pull of the three.

steps.title: Four chords in your key
steps.prompt:
Lay out a four-chord progression in your key:

1. Switch the slot strip to **2 / bar**. Now there are four slots: 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b.
2. Tap slot **1a**, then four pads in a row. Each pad fills the next slot.
3. Press play and listen.

Copy one of the four progressions, or make your own. Start on **i** so it sounds like home. At 2 / bar each chord lasts half a bar, so it moves twice as fast as the examples.
hints: At **1 / bar** there are only two slots. Switch the strip to **2 / bar** to get four, then tap slot **1a** before you tap the pads.

Every pad's basic chord counts as in key, **V ·borrowed** included. If the check names a note outside your key, it probably came from a **9**, **sus2** or **sus4** picked by holding a pad. Hold that pad, pick **Triad**, and place it again.
In a minor key, try **i, VI, III, VII**: in A minor that's Am, F, C, G. Tap slot 1a, then those four pads in order.

steps.message: Practice rep, so nothing goes into Your Track. Next lesson you'll pick chords for your own melody, and those you keep.
